title.narrative: 2021 - 2026 Core programmatic support to monitor and safeguard an enabling environment for civil society

description.narrative: The Dutch Government's programmatic funding to CIVICUS contributes to the policy goal of monitoring and safeguarding an enabling environment for civil society of the Department for Social Development (DSO) (policy article 3.3 strengthening civil society). Besides, the proposed cooperation with CIVICUS fits in the policy goals as described in the policy letter to Parliament of the Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation of 9 October 2013. CIVICUS plays different roles as monitoring, lobbying, and convening, within the international discussion on enabling environment for civil society. CIVICUS has access to international networks and policy processes, and stimulates democratization of these processes. Besides, CIVICUS produces yearly, relevant and up-to-date research and monitoring reports. It is important for civil society worldwide and for the MFA that these roles and products are supported in order to maintain quality. Besides, the roles that CIVICUS plays are very complementary to the roles that the MFA plays and can increasingly play in international discussions. CIVICUS also complements the roles international and Dutch civil society play in capacity strengthening for both Lobby and Advocacy and for service delivery. CIVICUS tackles the basic conditions for civil society to operate at both national and international level.

recipient-country.narrative: CIVICUS' headquarters are based in Johannesburg, South Africa, but the organisation operates worldwide.

comment.narrative: CIVICUS supports civil society to advocate for positive change through technical, networking, financial and other resources. Below are the outcomes that we captured that our support contributed towards: 1) A significant win from the #StandAsMyWitness campaign: seven human rights defenders (HRDs) profiled were released. These include Tatsiana Lasitsa, Leanid Sudalenka, and Andrei Chapiuk from the Viasna group in Belarus, as well as Kamira Nait Sid from Algeria.2) From our #StandAsMyWitness campaign: In Guatemala, Claudia González was released and placed under house arrest, and Virginia Laparra—also initially placed under house arrest upon her release on January 3, 2024—ultimately went into exile in early 2025 following renewed legal threats and the risk of re-incarceration. While challenges remain, these releases represent important progress and impact driven by sustained advocacy efforts. As agreed, we report 30% of the total number of results on IATI. CIVICUS supports civil society to advocate for positive change through technical, networking, financial and other resources. Below are the outcomes that we captured that our support contributed towards:1.Indonesia (January 2024) Prominent Indonesian human rights defenders Fatia Maulidiyanti and Haris Azhar were acquitted. The pair were charged in March 2022 for defamation. Even before the charges were laid, a focused campaign supported by CIVICUS mobilised civil society to call for the investigation be dropped and their acquittal. The campaign ended successfully when, on 8 January 2024, the East Jakarta District Court found that their actions did not amount to defamation and acquitted them of all charges.2.(Guatamala, January 2024) Minister of Mines and Energy appointment halted as a result of civil society pushback. In response to the public denouncement during the live event, civil society mobilized promptly. Statements were issued, and there was a concerted effort to push back against the candidacy of the Minister of Energy and Mines. The collective action from civil society resulted in her resignation, signalling not only a victory for human rights advocates but also a broader indication of the new government's commitment to advancing a human rights agenda. This episode serves as a tangible example of how strategic events, organized in a timely manner and supported by partnerships, can play a crucial role in making problems visible and driving positive action. It highlights the interconnectedness of advocacy, information dissemination, and public mobilization in the pursuit of a more just and rights-respecting society.3.CIVICUS Alliance is a thought partner to USAID and to US philanthropy organisations committed to advancing locally led development and shifting power /resources to CS groups on the ground. The insider/outsider strategy makes our alliance a credible and legitimate interlocutor on this change agenda. As agreed, we report 30% of the total number of results on IATI. This reflects the multiple donors that contribute to the activities supporting the outcomes. CIVICUS supports civil society to advocate for positive change through technical, networking, financial and other resources. Below are the outcome that we captured that our support contribution towards:1.Zambia: The passing and adoption of Access to Information Law (ATI) since it was first introduced in parliament 20 years ago. On 15 December 2023, the Zambian parliament finally adopted the Access to Information Act into law, following years of public debate about the importance of such legislation.2.Zambia: The amendment of the Penal Code. In October 2022, Zambia’s Cabinet approved a review of the penal and criminal procedure codes. The Bill was then debated in Parliament before being passed in December. On 23 December 2023, President Hichilema signed the Bill, which does not have retrospective effect, into law. In February 2023, the President commuted 390 death sentences to life imprisonment. As such, there are reportedly no longer any individuals on death row in Zambia.As agreed, we report 30% of the total number of results on IATI. CIVICUS supports civil society to advocate for positive change through technical, networking, financial and other resources. Below is the outcome that we captured that our support contribution towards:Malawi’s High Court (sitting as a Constitutional Court) declaring Section 200 of the Malawi Penal Code, which criminalised defamation, unconstitutional. The Court ruled that the law which made defamation a criminal offence is against the country’s Constitution. The court said the law unfairly limits people’s freedom to speak freely, especially in a democracy. CIVICUS, through CHARM contributed to this cause through the UPR reports of 2021 and 2025, with mid-stream advocacy work, including diplomatic defenders’ dialogue held in 2024, plus capacity skilling trainings on advocacy, and technical support to partners. The ruling is key and a right path in paving way for free civic space in the country. title.narrative: SCS4 # of advocacy initiatives carried out by CSOs, for, by or with their membership/constituency

description.narrative: Our analysis of civil society trends clearly points to the emergence of new frontiers. Many of today’s movements centre on a new generation of people who are creating their own structures of participation and activism. These mobilisations, often fluid and non-hierarchical in nature, include young people exercising their civic freedoms for the first time and people from excluded groups reasserting the value of their worldviews. An upsurge in popular protests and social movements, coupled with the rise of social enterprises spurred by technological innovations, is transforming the civil society landscape.

Our ultimate goal is to strengthen citizen action and civil society that expands civic and democratic space. The outcomes that will contribute to this goal are underpinned by our strategic objectives, which articulate CIVICUS’s unique approach to achieving the breakthroughs we want to see through enabling lasting and transformative change across the varied and interconnected aspects of our work.Our unique value lies in our ability to make use of the combined approaches of (1) generating knowledge and timely analysis, (2) amplifying civil society narratives, (3) influencing policy making, (4) enabling activism in challenging contexts and (5) strengthening solidarity action through strategic alliances and innovative partnerships.We believe that this can be achieved through creating systemic shifts in policy, practice and public narratives, which help to bring about more transformative, sustainable change.

We intend to strengthen the efficacy, credibility, legitimacy and influence of citizen and civil society action to claim fundamental civic rights and resist oppressive power through the following actions:1.Improved ability of excluded groups to challenge oppressive power and transform policy making:•There is increased recognition of the role of collective action by excluded groups in achieving sustained change •There is a shift of funding, support and solidarity towards groups that are most affected by the combined impact of civic and democratic space restrictions and structural forms of discrimination2.Improved public discourse that reflects greater value for civic and democratic space and social and environmental justice, and greater recognition of the relevance and sustained impact of civil society:•Locally led public deliberations and context-relevant analyses are provided in diverse locations and languages around the world•Greater public trust is reflected through increased solidarity with the work and priorities of the CIVICUS alliance and broader civil society3.Improved accountability by decision makers to uphold the fundamental civic freedoms of association, peaceful assembly and expression:• More actions are taken to support and expand democratic participation in decision-making processes with a focus on citizen and civil society engagement across borders and at scale•There is evidence that institutional policies and legislation are becoming more supportive of a vibrant, autonomous civil society4.Increased and more effective civil society action moves decision makers to safeguard and expand civic and democratic space:•All forms of civil society find more innovative and effective ways to create transnational and cross-thematic opportunities for solidarity action•Citizens and civil society leverage knowledge, research and analysis to advance organising and influencing efforts and hold decision makers accountable at local, national, regional and global levels•Advocacy and lobbying are done in more empowering and transformative ways to better hold public and private institutions accountable

title.narrative: SCS3 # of times that CSOs succeed in creating space for CSO demands and positions through agenda setting, influencing the debate and/or creating space to engage.

description.narrative: The space for civil society to promote rights and pursue social justice has been historically contested. But presently, we’re seeing a greater range of states attacking civil society, the rise of anti-rights groups and a sharpening of tactics of restriction, including online attacks and censorship. Many contexts have seen political upheaval and a rejection of norms around the conduct of politics and democracy.
